Trojanized npm Packages Employ NullReceiver Tactic to Decode C2 IP from Blockchain

The Hacker News
2026-08-05 10 use cases 5 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged an evolution of the EtherHiding blockchain-based command-and-control (C2) technique that conceals the C2 server IP address inside a made-up destination address of a completely empty Ethereum transfer. The new dead drop resolver approach, observed in two trojanized npm packages "bianira-ui" and "fluid-type-ui," has been codenamed NullReceiver by

NullReceiver npm C2 beacon to hardcoded IP 166.88.134.62 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any host connecting outbound to 166.88.134.62, the C2 server that the trojanized npm packages bianira-ui and fluid-type-ui decode from the recipient bytes (a6 58 86 3e) of a zero-value Ethereum transfer. Because the packages impersonate front-end Tailwind/CSS UI libraries, a node process reaching this raw IP is unambiguously malicious. Rationale: 166.88.134.62 is a hardcoded network IOC confirmed by three independent write-ups (cybersecuritynews, gbhackers, cyberpress) and the OpenSourceMalware decode flowchart, giving it near-zero false-positive risk as a direct-match alert. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/north-korean-hackers-hiding-malware/ • https://gbhackers.com/nullreceiver-wallet-trail/ • https://cyberpress.org/nullreceiver-hides-ethereum-c2/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internal asset legitimately assigned 166.88.134.62 after attacker infrastructure is sinkholed/reassigned (verify current WHOIS/ASN)
  • Security researcher or sandbox detonating the sample intentionally
  • Threat-intel proxy or TAXII feed proactively probing the IOC
  • NAT egress where the IP is a shared upstream (rare for a /32 attacker host)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcessCommandLine/process — expect node.exe/npm; pull the host's node_modules for bianira-ui or fluid-type-ui and the developer/user who ran the install. 2) Contain: block 166.88.134.62 at the egress firewall/EDR, isolate the host, and revoke any developer/CI credentials and npm tokens that lived on the box (DPRK Contagious Interview targets dev secrets). 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints and CI runners for outbound hits to this IP and for the two package names, and pivot on the attacker wallet 0xa322e5f3d311d3080e6f0121063e9adc2490ef1a to enumerate rotated C2 IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "166.88.134.62"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "166.88.134.62"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DstHostname, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Install of trojanized npm packages bianira-ui / fluid-type-ui AIInstallation High
Hunts file writes into node_modules for the two known-malicious packages bianira-ui (by npmuser1101) and fluid-type-ui (by npmuser3002), which masquerade as Tailwind CSS plugins. Catches the supply-chain foothold at install time on developer workstations and CI runners regardless of the C2 IP, which rotates. Rationale: Package names bianira-ui and fluid-type-ui are corroborated by the original THN report plus cybersecuritynews and gbhackers; matching the node_modules install path yields a high-fidelity, IP-rotation-resistant detection that fires on the supply-chain foothold itself. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/north-korean-hackers-hiding-malware/ • https://gbhackers.com/nullreceiver-wallet-trail/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign package coincidentally named with the same string in an unrelated scoped path (unlikely given exact names)
  • Security team intentionally st[ag]ing the sample in a malware lab
  • Internal mirror/Artifactory caching the withdrawn package for IR analysis
  • Developer restoring an old lockfile that still references the removed package
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the installing user and whether the package reached a runtime (node/npm parent) versus only lockfile resolution; grab package.json/package-lock.json to see how it entered the dependency tree. 2) Contain: uninstall the package, isolate the host/CI runner, rotate npm tokens, SSH keys, cloud creds and wallet keys present on the box, and purge any internal registry cache copies. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1 (outbound to 166.88.134.62), search all lockfiles across repos for the two names, and check for other packages from npmuser1101 and npmuser3002.

NullReceiver dead-drop: node queries Ethereum RPC then beacons to a raw IP AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the NullReceiver resolution behaviour itself: a node/npm process contacts a public Ethereum RPC provider (to read the attacker wallet's last transaction) and, within 5 minutes on the same host, connects to a raw public IP with no DNS/hostname — the decoded C2. This survives C2-IP and wallet rotation and flags copycat packages the IOCs miss. Rationale: The OpenSourceMalware flowchart (null.png) confirms the sequence npm package -> public Ethereum ledger lookup -> connect to decoded raw IP; correlating a node RPC read with a same-host connection to a hostname-less public IP within 5 min captures the technique generically, catching rotated wallets/IPs that pure IOC rules miss. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/trojanized-npm-packages-decode-c2-ip.html • https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhp2JlYxtO8ERLKOUQWEHhsEpf5fOczPAzfCYSUfZJCs4_O3vxIogUH1sH3pDS3TnpeQ9ctxXu0QVfTQTdt9I_BfsYl8SaF5cpY_wKimW9-tkgLOE4tYnUr7aSVDnM4d0CEMr4pYT5KiV-_mCYQMzC_vhwRQDTUunVBKiBKjgFiAPMs_A1TSBlWubYasQHK/s1700-e365/null.png
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate web3/dapp or wallet-integration project whose node backend polls an Ethereum RPC then opens raw-IP peer connections
  • Blockchain indexer / node client (ethers.js, web3.js, hardhat) running in dev or CI
  • Crypto price-ticker or NFT tooling that reads on-chain data
  • P2P libraries (libp2p, IPFS) that dial peers by IP after a bootstrap lookup
Suppression filter
// Suppress known-good web3 projects by initiating command line / working dir
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("hardhat", "truffle", "ethers", "web3", "foundry", "ganache")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the node process's working directory and package.json — a UI/CSS-themed dependency (like Tailwind plugins) that touches Ethereum RPC is the tell; capture the raw IP it dialed. 2) Contain: block the decoded raw IP and the parent package, isolate the host, and rotate developer/CI secrets. 3) Hunt: enrich the raw IP against threat intel, pivot the host's process tree for the trojanized package names, and add the newly-observed C2 IP and any new attacker wallet addresses to the IOC watchlist for org-wide sweeping.
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let WindowSec = 300;
let RpcHosts = dynamic(["mainnet.infura.io","eth-mainnet.g.alchemy.com","cloudflare-eth.com","rpc.ankr.com","ethereum.publicnode.com","api.etherscan.io","etherscan.io","eth.llamarpc.com","bsc-dataseed.binance.org","rpc.flashbots.net"]);
let BlockchainLookups = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","npm")
    | where RemoteUrl has_any (RpcHosts)
    | project RpcTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, RpcHost = RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where isempty(RemoteUrl)
| join kind=inner BlockchainLookups on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (RpcTime .. RpcTime + WindowSec * 1s)
| project RpcTime, RawIpTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, RpcHost, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by RawIpTime desc
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let WindowSec = 300;
let RpcHosts = dynamic(["mainnet.infura.io","eth-mainnet.g.alchemy.com","cloudflare-eth.com","rpc.ankr.com","ethereum.publicnode.com","api.etherscan.io","etherscan.io","eth.llamarpc.com","bsc-dataseed.binance.org","rpc.flashbots.net"]);
let BlockchainLookups = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where DstHostname has_any (RpcHosts)
    | project RpcTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, RpcHost = DstHostname;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where isempty(DstHostname) and isnotempty(DstIpAddr)
| join kind=inner BlockchainLookups on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (RpcTime .. RpcTime + WindowSec * 1s)
| project RpcTime, RawIpTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RpcHost, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| order by RawIpTime desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New OVSwrap Linux Kernel Flaw Lets Local Users Gain Root via Open vSwitch

The Hacker News
2026-08-05 10 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A memory corruption flaw in the Linux kernel's Open vSwitch datapath gives ordinary local users a path to root on a broad set of default-configured distributions, and a public exploit ships with pre-built records for roughly 800 kernel builds. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-64531 (CVSS score: 7.8) and codenamed OVSwrap by its discoverer, was disclosed by security researcher Asim

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] OVSwrap privesc: unprivileged `unshare -Urn` to obtain CAP_NET_ADMIN in new netns · [LLM] OVSwrap: openvswitch kernel module load/autoload on a host that doesn't run ovs-vswitchd · [LLM] OVSwrap AppArmor bypass: `aa-exec -p trinity` userns-restriction fallback (Ubuntu 24.04) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] OVSwrap post-exploit: /etc/sudoers or /etc/sudoers.d modified outside package/config tooling · Article-specific behavioural hunt — New OVSwrap Linux Kernel Flaw Lets Local Users Gain Root via Open vSwitch
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
OVSwrap privesc: unprivileged `unshare -Urn` to obtain CAP_NET_ADMIN in new netns AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the OVSwrap (CVE-2026-64531) entry step where an ordinary local user runs `unshare -Urn` to create private user+network namespaces and gain CAP_NET_ADMIN inside them, the prerequisite for reaching the vulnerable Open vSwitch flow-installation path. This is the exact invocation the public PoC uses to start the chain on default-configured distros. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact PoC command `unshare -Urn` (creating user+network namespaces to gain CAP_NET_ADMIN); non-root actor excludes normal privileged container tooling. Corroborated against CloudLinux and securityonline write-ups of the same PoC. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.cloudlinux.com/ovswrap-cve-2026-64531-mitigation/ • https://securityonline.info/ovswrap-cve-2026-64531-local-root/ • https://cloudlinux.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/29223197225116-Kernel-Local-Privilege-Escalation-CVE-2026-64531-OVSwrap-Open-vSwitch-Affected-Status-and-Fix
ATT&CKT1068 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Container runtimes (Podman/rootless Docker, LXC, bubblewrap) legitimately creating user+net namespaces
  • CI/CD sandboxing jobs using unshare for isolation
  • Developers testing network namespaces manually
  • Flatpak/snap application launches that spin up namespaces
  • nsenter/unshare used by systemd or debugging tooling
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("podman","dockerd","containerd","runc","lxc-start","bwrap","flatpak","snap","systemd")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the unshare PID on the host — is the parent an interactive shell of a non-service user, and does an openvswitch module load or sudoers write follow within seconds? 2) Contain: if the actor is untrusted/multi-tenant, freeze the account, snapshot the host, and apply the module block `echo 'install openvswitch /bin/false' > /etc/modprobe.d/ovswrap.conf` then unload/reboot. 3) Hunt: search the same host and user for subsequent `modprobe/insmod openvswitch`, `aa-exec -p trinity`, and writes to /etc/sudoers* — confirming the OVSwrap chain vs. benign namespace usage.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "unshare"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-Urn","-rUn","-Unr") or (ProcessCommandLine has "--user" and ProcessCommandLine has "--net" and (ProcessCommandLine has "--map-root-user" or ProcessCommandLine has "-r"))
| where AccountName != "root" and AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "/unshare" or TargetProcessName == "unshare"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("-Urn","-rUn") or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "--user" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "--net")
| where ActorUsername != "root"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OVSwrap: openvswitch kernel module load/autoload on a host that doesn't run ovs-vswitchd AIExploitation Medium
Hunts loading of the vulnerable openvswitch datapath module via modprobe/insmod — the OVSwrap exploit triggers auto-load by resolving the Generic Netlink family name, so the module can appear even where lsmod was previously empty and ovs-vswitchd is not deployed. On non-OVS/OpenStack hosts this load is anomalous and a direct signal of CVE-2026-64531 exploitation prep. Rationale: Uses the article's specific module name `openvswitch` and the auto-load-by-genl-family behaviour it calls out; scoping to hosts that don't run ovs-vswitchd makes the module load high-signal. Confirmed as the exploited component in SentinelOne and CloudLinux advisories. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-64531/ • https://cloudlinux.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/29223197225116-Kernel-Local-Privilege-Escalation-CVE-2026-64531-OVSwrap-Open-vSwitch-Affected-Status-and-Fix
ATT&CKT1547.006 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate OpenStack / OVN / OVS hypervisor and network nodes loading openvswitch at boot
  • systemd-modules-load.service or /etc/modules-load.d loading OVS on networking hosts
  • Kubernetes CNI plugins (e.g. OVN-Kubernetes, Antrea) loading the datapath
  • Admin manually enabling Open vSwitch for a new bridge
  • Configuration-management (Ansible/Puppet) provisioning OVS on network infra
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in (dynamic(["ovs-node-01","ovs-node-02"])) and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("systemd","systemd-modules-load","ansible","puppet")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host is a legitimate OVS/OpenStack/OVN/CNI node (is ovs-vswitchd installed and enabled?). If not, treat the load as suspicious. 2) Contain: on non-OVS hosts, deploy `echo 'install openvswitch /bin/false' > /etc/modprobe.d/ovswrap.conf`, then unload the resident module (`modprobe -r openvswitch`) or schedule a reboot; isolate if multi-tenant. 3) Hunt: correlate a preceding `unshare -Urn` by a non-root user and any following /etc/sudoers* writes or new root shells on the same host to confirm the OVSwrap chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("modprobe","insmod","kmod")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "openvswitch"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Loads=count(),
            SampleCmd=any(ProcessCommandLine), Parents=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 5)
            by DeviceName, AccountName, FileName
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/modprobe","/insmod","/kmod") or TargetProcessName in~ ("modprobe","insmod","kmod")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "openvswitch"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OVSwrap AppArmor bypass: `aa-exec -p trinity` userns-restriction fallback (Ubuntu 24.04) AIExploitation High
Detects the OVSwrap PoC's AppArmor bypass fallback — where direct namespace creation is blocked on Ubuntu 24.04, the exploit re-runs itself under the permissive `trinity` profile via `aa-exec -p trinity` to restore reachability to the vulnerable path. The `aa-exec -p trinity` string is a near-unique PoC artifact. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact PoC artifact `aa-exec -p trinity`, an AppArmor-confinement bypass specific to the OVSwrap exploit on Ubuntu 24.04 — extremely unlikely to appear in benign administration. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/new-ovswrap-linux-kernel-flaw-lets.html • https://pbxscience.com/ovswrap-flaw-in-linux-kernels-open-vswitch-lets-local-users-become-root/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A site that legitimately ships a custom AppArmor profile literally named 'trinity'
  • Security researchers reproducing the OVSwrap PoC in an authorized lab
  • AppArmor profile testing/QA that invokes aa-exec with a named profile
  • Automated exploit-detection or vuln-scanning tooling replaying the PoC
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is near-unique to the PoC — immediately confirm the host, actor, and whether a 'trinity' AppArmor profile even legitimately exists there (`aa-status`). 2) Contain: isolate the host, freeze the invoking account, capture memory/process tree; on Ubuntu re-enable the userns AppArmor restriction and apply the openvswitch module block. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for the full chain — preceding `unshare -Urn`, openvswitch module load, and following /etc/sudoers* modification or unexpected uid=0 shells.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "aa-exec"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "trinity"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-p","--profile")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "/aa-exec" or TargetProcessName == "aa-exec"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "trinity" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("-p","--profile")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OVSwrap post-exploit: /etc/sudoers or /etc/sudoers.d modified outside package/config tooling AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the OVSwrap PoC's post-root action — after corrupting a kernel credential it modifies /etc/sudoers.d or /etc/sudoers to entrench root access before opening a root shell. Flags writes to these paths by processes that are not the sanctioned sudoers editors or package/config-management tooling. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit post-exploit action — the PoC modifies /etc/sudoers.d or /etc/sudoers to persist root — and filters the known-good editors/package managers so only anomalous writers surface. Datadog left empty: the linux.auditd standard schema exposes process/user fields but not a reliable file-path attribute for this write. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/new-ovswrap-linux-kernel-flaw-lets.html • https://blog.cloudlinux.com/ovswrap-cve-2026-64531-mitigation/
ATT&CKT1548.003 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Configuration management (Ansible/Puppet/Chef/Salt) deploying sudoers drop-ins
  • cloud-init seeding sudoers for a new cloud instance's default user
  • Admin adding a sudo rule via a text editor instead of visudo
  • Package post-install scripts dropping files into /etc/sudoers.d
  • IdM/SSSD or FreeIPA tooling syncing sudo rules
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("salt-minion","ansible","puppet","chef-client","cloud-init")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the newly written sudoers content and identify the writing process and user — a non-editor writer (e.g. an exploit binary or unexpected shell) adding NOPASSWD/ALL for a normal user is high-confidence malicious. 2) Contain: revert the sudoers change, revoke/reset the affected account, isolate the host and preserve the file plus process tree for forensics. 3) Hunt: correlate on the same host for the OVSwrap precursors — `unshare -Urn`, openvswitch module load, `aa-exec -p trinity` — and any root shell spawned immediately after the write; patch to a fixed vendor kernel.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath == "/etc/sudoers" or FolderPath startswith "/etc/sudoers.d/"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("visudo","sudoedit","apt","apt-get","dpkg","yum","dnf","rpm","puppet","chef-client","ansible","cloud-init","unattended-upgr")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath == "/etc/sudoers" or TargetFilePath startswith "/etc/sudoers.d/"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreate","FileWrite")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("visudo","sudoedit","apt","dpkg","yum","dnf","rpm","puppet","chef-client","ansible","cloud-init"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src

Kali365 Weaponizes Microsoft Authentication Against US Companies: New Enterprise Risk

The Hacker News
2026-08-05 9 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Kali365 is turning a legitimate Microsoft login into a gateway to corporate data. The phishing kit targets US organizations with attacker-controlled device codes that victims approve on Microsoft's real authentication page. Once access and refresh tokens are issued, attackers may retain access to email, documents, and cloud resources, creating a direct path to data exposure, financial fraud,

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Host or mailbox contact with Kali365 lure domains (SharePoint/OneDrive/DocuSign decoys) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Kali365 device-code-flow authentication used by a standard M365 user · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Kali365 concurrent device-code sign-in: same user, 2+ IPs/countries in one hour · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Kali365 device-code-flow authentication used by a standard M365 user AIExploitation Medium
Hunts successful Entra ID sign-ins that completed via the OAuth device-code grant, which Kali365 abuses to have victims approve an attacker-generated code on Microsoft's real login page. Device-code flow is legitimate but rare for interactive knowledge workers, making its appearance on a normal user account a high-value pivot for token theft. Rationale: Uses the article's core TTP — attacker-controlled device codes approved on Microsoft's legitimate device-login portal — expressed as the OAuth device-code grant, which is the single defining signal of Kali365 token issuance. AuthenticationProtocol not being an available column in this tenant's SigninLogs schema, the flow is matched on the deviceCode marker inside AuthenticationDetails. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/kali365-weaponizes-microsoft.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1621/
ATT&CKT1528 T1621
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineers authenticating Azure CLI / Azure PowerShell on a shell that cannot pop a browser
  • Conference-room / Teams Rooms and smart-TV devices enrolling via device code
  • IoT or headless kiosk provisioning that legitimately uses the device-code grant
  • Developers logging into az login --use-device-code over SSH
  • New MDM/Intune device onboarding using device-code sign-in
Suppression filter
| where not (Application has_any ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell") and DeviceTrustType == "Azure AD joined")
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the user's device-code sign-ins — check the resource/app requested, source IP geo, and whether the user owns a headless/CLI workflow that would explain it. Compare the sign-in IP to the user's normal locations. 2. Contain: if unexplained, revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession / 'Revoke sessions'), force password reset, and require re-MFA; block the source IP. 3. Hunt: enumerate all OAuth tokens/apps consented for the account, review mailbox rules and recent mail/file access, and search other users for device-code sign-ins from the same IP/ASN within 24h.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"   // device-code grant marker in the auth-detail JSON
| where ErrorCode == 0                            // completed sign-in => token issued
| where isnotempty(AccountUpn) and AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Countries = make_set(Country, 20),
            Apps = make_set(Application, 10), Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 10)
            by AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName
| order by LastSeen desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"   // device-code grant marker in AuthenticationDetails JSON
| where ResultType == 0                           // successful sign-in
| where isnotempty(UserPrincipalName)
| extend CountryOrRegion = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Countries = make_set(CountryOrRegion, 20),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10), Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 10)
            by UserPrincipalName, UserDisplayName
| order by LastSeen desc

id: 6f2b1c94-2e77-4a1d-9c5a-8b0d3f7e2a11
description: Detects successful Entra ID sign-ins completed via the OAuth device-code grant, abused by the Kali365 phishing kit for token theft.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/kali365-weaponizes-microsoft.html
  - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/05
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1528
  - attack.t1621
logsource:
  product: azure
  service: signinlogs
detection:
  selection:
    AuthenticationProtocol: deviceCode
    ResultType: 0
  condition: selection
level: medium
CLOUD
sourcetype="azure:aad:signin" "properties.authenticationProtocol"="deviceCode" "properties.status.errorCode"=0
| stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values("properties.ipAddress") as ipAddress values("properties.appDisplayName") as app values("properties.resourceDisplayName") as resource dc("properties.ipAddress") as ipCount by user
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

Kali365 concurrent device-code sign-in: same user, 2+ IPs/countries in one hour AICommand & Control Medium
Correlates successful device-code-flow sign-ins for a single user across two or more distinct IPs or countries within a one-hour window — the pattern seen when a victim approves the code from their location while the Kali365 operator uses the issued token from separate infrastructure. Adds temporal + geo divergence on top of the raw device-code signal to raise fidelity. Rationale: Builds on the article's device-code abuse by adding the operational tell that the person approving the code and the person using the resulting token are in different places — 2+ IPs/countries for the same user in a 1h device-code window. Correlation/threshold shape, so Sigma is intentionally omitted. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/kali365-weaponizes-microsoft.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/004/
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Traveling user whose VPN egress and local carrier IP both appear within the hour
  • Mobile users roaming between Wi-Fi and cellular NAT pools mapped to different geos
  • Corporate proxy / cloud-egress that presents multiple regional IPs for one session
  • Legitimate CLI auth from a datacenter jump host while the user is also at their desk
  • Geo-IP database inaccuracy splitting a single ISP block across two countries
Response runbook
1. Triage: list the two+ IPs and their ASNs/geos for the flagged hour; determine which IP matches the user's known device/location and whether the other is a hosting/VPS provider (operator infra). 2. Contain: revoke refresh tokens and sessions for the account, force password reset + re-MFA, and add the non-user IP/ASN to conditional-access block. 3. Hunt: pivot on the suspicious IP across all users for device-code sign-ins, review the account's OAuth grants, inbox rules, and file/mail access since first-seen; check for token replay against Exchange/SharePoint from the same IP.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where isnotempty(AccountUpn) and AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| summarize IPs = dcount(IPAddress), Countries = dcount(Country),
            IPList = make_set(IPAddress, 20), CountryList = make_set(Country, 20),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where IPs >= 2 or Countries >= 2   // victim approves locally, operator uses token from other infra
| order by LastSeen desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"
| where ResultType == 0
| where isnotempty(UserPrincipalName)
| extend CountryOrRegion = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)
| summarize IPs = dcount(IPAddress), Countries = dcount(CountryOrRegion),
            IPList = make_set(IPAddress, 20), CountryList = make_set(CountryOrRegion, 20),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where IPs >= 2 or Countries >= 2   // victim approves locally, operator uses token from other infra
| order by LastSeen desc
CLOUD
sourcetype="azure:aad:signin" "properties.authenticationProtocol"="deviceCode" "properties.status.errorCode"=0
| bin _time span=1h
| stats dc("properties.ipAddress") as ipCount dc("location.countryOrRegion") as countryCount values("properties.ipAddress") as ips values("location.countryOrRegion") as countries by user, _time
| where ipCount>=2 OR countryCount>=2
| sort - _time
Host or mailbox contact with Kali365 lure domains (SharePoint/OneDrive/DocuSign decoys) AIDelivery High
Matches endpoint web/DNS traffic and delivered email URLs against the confirmed Kali365 lure-hosting domains that impersonate SharePoint, OneDrive and DocuSign to funnel victims into the device-code flow. This is the earliest detectable stage — the lure/redirect — before any Microsoft token is issued. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the article's pre-extracted Kali365 lure domains — high fidelity because these are dedicated attacker-registered domains with no legitimate business use; catches the lure/redirect stage before a token is ever issued. Covers DNS, endpoint web egress, and mail-delivered URLs. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/kali365-weaponizes-microsoft.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst detonating the lure URL in a sandbox from a corporate endpoint
  • Threat-intel enrichment / URL-scanning tooling resolving the domains for feeds
  • A previously-benign domain being sinkholed and now resolving to a research IP
  • User forwarding the phishing mail internally causing repeated URL clicks by responders
  • Newly-parked domain reuse where the string collides with an unrelated legitimate host (validate WHOIS)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the user/device that resolved or browsed the domain and whether a device-code sign-in followed within the next 30 minutes (join to UC1 signal). Confirm the domain is still live/malicious. 2. Contain: block all 20 domains at proxy/DNS/firewall and quarantine the delivering email tenant-wide; if a sign-in followed, revoke the user's tokens and force MFA reset. 3. Hunt: search email, web and DNS across the org for any of the domains, expand to newly-registered look-alike SharePoint/OneDrive/DocuSign domains on the same registrar/ASN, and push the IOCs to SIEM/TIP for retrospective search.
let Kali365Domains = dynamic(["bluefoodtruths.xyz","flexiscalesystems.de","guardedwebsolutions.de","proforcstaffing.com","reputationboosters.de","guardextion.online","prowebsitemakers.de","onlinebrandinghub.de","onsite-developments.net","functionalityfirst.de","buildyouronlineidentity.de","flexievolve.de","onlineidentityperfection.de","guardwebsolutions.de","securedecisionmaking.de","modernwebbalance.de","marketadaptabletech.de","waschmaschinenmarkt.de","hbaknoxvillecom.top","brandswithintegrity.de"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (Kali365Domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let Kali365Domains = dynamic(["bluefoodtruths.xyz","flexiscalesystems.de","guardedwebsolutions.de","proforcstaffing.com","reputationboosters.de","guardextion.online","prowebsitemakers.de","onlinebrandinghub.de","onsite-developments.net","functionalityfirst.de","buildyouronlineidentity.de","flexievolve.de","onlineidentityperfection.de","guardwebsolutions.de","securedecisionmaking.de","modernwebbalance.de","marketadaptabletech.de","waschmaschinenmarkt.de","hbaknoxvillecom.top","brandswithintegrity.de"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| extend UrlHost = tolower(tostring(parse_url(Url).Host))
| where UrlHost in (Kali365Domains)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, SrcHostname, Url, UrlHost, DstIpAddr, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Kali365 Lure Domain DNS Resolution
id: b1e7d3a2-9c44-4f81-a0d6-5c2e9f14b7c3
description: Detects DNS resolution of Kali365 device-code phishing lure domains impersonating SharePoint/OneDrive/DocuSign.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/kali365-weaponizes-microsoft.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/05
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1566.002
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:

#event_simpleName=DnsRequest

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"

   or ParentProcessName endswith "\visio.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |
    User-driven consent to a third-party OAuth application — illicit-

references:

Critical Gitea Flaw Let Unauthenticated Attackers Read Server Files via Org-Mode Markup

The Hacker News
2026-08-05 8 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

An unauthenticated attacker can read any file the service account can access on Gitea, the self-hosted Git platform, in versions 1.22.1 through 1.27.0. No login, no repository write access. A public repository and crafted Org-mode markup are enough. The flaw is fixed in Gitea 1.27.1. The file-read flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-59774, rated Critical with a CVSS score of 9.8, and received its

CVEsCVE-2026-59774 CVE-2026-60004 CVE-2026-20896 CVE-2026-27771
ATT&CKT1190 T1528 T1566 T1566.002

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Anonymous POST to Gitea Org-mode markup endpoint (CVE-2026-59774 file-read) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Gitea process spawning unexpected shell/tooling from a hook (CVE-2026-59774 token-to-hook escalation)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Anonymous POST to Gitea Org-mode markup endpoint (CVE-2026-59774 file-read) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts unauthenticated POST requests to Gitea's /{owner}/{repo}/markup rendering endpoint, the file-read primitive in CVE-2026-59774 where an Org-mode #+INCLUDE directive with an absolute path (Mode: file) coerces the vulnerable go-org ReadFile callback (ioutil.ReadFile) into returning arbitrary server files (e.g. app.ini and its INTERNAL_TOKEN) readable by the Gitea service account. Article-specific because it keys on the exact vulnerable route and the anonymous-access precondition against a public repo with the code unit enabled. Rationale: Anchors on the exact vulnerable route POST /{owner}/{repo}/markup plus the anonymous-user precondition the advisory names; scStatus 200 confirms the render succeeded. Request body (Mode: file / absolute path) isn't in access logs, so we alert on the endpoint+anon+success triad. Cross-checked against the Gitea advisory and go-gitea PR #38642/#38645 cited in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/38642 • https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/38645 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-59774
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001 T1005
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated users using the Gitea web-UI live markdown/Org preview where the reverse proxy logs an empty/'-' username
  • External vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Nuclei) probing the markup route
  • Uptime/health-check bots POSTing to Gitea paths
  • CI integrations that render markup anonymously against public repos
  • Security researchers re-testing the patch after upgrade to 1.27.1
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has "Qualys" and csUserAgent !has "Nessus" and csUserAgent !has "nuclei" and csUserAgent !has "Nmap"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target Gitea build is 1.22.1–1.27.0 (vulnerable) and that scStatus=200; pull the full request from the reverse proxy/WAF to see whether the POST body contains Org-mode '#+INCLUDE' with 'Mode: file' or an absolute path (e.g. app.ini). Note the source IP and repeat cadence. 2) Contain: upgrade to 1.27.1 immediately; block the offending source IP at the proxy; treat all secrets readable by the Gitea service account as exposed and rotate INTERNAL_TOKEN, OAuth material, JWT signing keys, and DB credentials. 3) Hunt: search hook directories under gitea-repositories for unexpected executables and pivot to UC 'Gitea process spawning unexpected interpreter' for the token→hook escalation.
// Gitea commonly fronted by IIS/nginx/WAF; this targets IIS W3C logs. For nginx use Syslog, for a WAF use CommonSecurityLog (RequestMethod/RequestURL/SourceUserName).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem endswith "/markup"
| where csUsername == "-" or isempty(csUsername)   // anonymous / unauthenticated
| where scStatus == 200
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, Computer, csMethod, csUriStem, csUsername, scStatus, csUserAgent, sSiteName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gitea process spawning unexpected shell/tooling from a hook (CVE-2026-59774 token-to-hook escalation) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the escalation chain in CVE-2026-59774 where a leaked INTERNAL_TOKEN is used to inject a Git hook via the internal logger, then triggered during an anonymous clone. Detects the Gitea/git server process spawning an interpreter or network tool (bash, sh, python, perl, nc, curl, wget) whose command line references a hooks path, gitea-repositories, /tmp, or a /dev/tcp reverse shell — behaviour that does not occur during a normal read-only clone. Rationale: The advisory's escalation is INTERNAL_TOKEN -> injected hook -> triggered on anonymous clone; a read-only clone should never cause the Gitea server to spawn an interpreter or a /dev/tcp reverse shell. Keys on the gitea/git parent plus interpreter child plus hook/gitea-repositories/tmp/dev-tcp command-line context, excluding legit git-lfs/git-shell helpers. Chain is single-sourced to Gitea's advisory, hence hunting tier. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/38642 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-59774
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate custom server-side Git hooks (pre-receive/post-receive/update) that call curl or wget for CI/webhook notifications
  • git-lfs or git-shell helper processes spawned during push/pull
  • Admin maintenance or migration scripts operating under gitea-repositories
  • Backup jobs reading repo trees including hooks directories
  • Gitea internal hooks writing to /tmp during large-repo operations
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("git-lfs","git-shell","git rev-list","git pack-objects"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line and the referenced hook file under gitea-repositories/<owner>/<repo>.git/hooks/ (or custom_hooks/); confirm the file is unexpected, recently created, and not part of a configured webhook. Correlate the host/time with UC1 anonymous /markup hits. 2) Contain: isolate the Gitea host, kill the process, quarantine the malicious hook file, and rotate INTERNAL_TOKEN/OAuth/JWT/DB credentials since a token leak precedes this stage; upgrade to 1.27.1. 3) Hunt: enumerate all repos' hook directories for other planted executables, review outbound connections from the gitea process for C2, and check for new admin users or SSH keys added post-compromise.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("gitea","git")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","python","python3","perl","nc","ncat","curl","wget")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("hooks/","gitea-repositories","/tmp/","/dev/tcp")
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "git-lfs" and ProcessCommandLine !has "git-shell"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("gitea","git")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","python","python3","perl","nc","ncat","curl","wget")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("hooks/","gitea-repositories","/tmp/","/dev/tcp")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has "git-lfs" and ActingProcessCommandLine !has "git-shell"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Gitea Server Process Spawning Unexpected Interpreter from Hook Path (CVE-2026-59774 escalation)
id: b21d4c6e-8a17-4f3b-9c02-71e5a9d3f884
description: Detects the Gitea/git server process spawning a shell or network tool whose command line references a hook path, gitea-repositories, /tmp, or /dev/tcp - the token-to-hook command-execution escalation of CVE-2026-59774.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/critical-gitea-flaw-let-unauthenticated.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/05
tags:
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1190
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/gitea'
      - '/git'
    Image|endswith:
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
      - '/dash'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/perl'
      - '/nc'
      - '/ncat'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
  context:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'hooks/'
      - 'gitea-repositories'
      - '/tmp/'
      - '/dev/tcp'
  condition: selection and context
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate custom Git server-side hooks invoking curl/wget for CI webhooks
  - git-lfs / git-shell helper invocations
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(bash OR sh OR dash OR python OR python3 OR perl OR nc OR ncat OR curl OR wget) (@process.command_line:(*hooks/* OR *gitea-repositories* OR */tmp/* OR */dev/tcp*)) -@process.command_line:(*git-lfs* OR *git-shell*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(gitea|git)$/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(bash|sh|dash|python3?|perl|nc|ncat|curl|wget)$/i
| regex("(hooks/|gitea-repositories|/tmp/|/dev/tcp)", field=CommandLine)
| NOT regex("(git-lfs|git-shell)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name=gitea OR Processes.parent_process_name=git) (Processes.process_name=bash OR Processes.process_name=sh OR Processes.process_name=dash OR Processes.process_name=python OR Processes.process_name=python3 OR Processes.process_name=perl OR Processes.process_name=nc OR Processes.process_name=ncat OR Processes.process_name=curl OR Processes.process_name=wget) (Processes.process="*hooks/*" OR Processes.process="*gitea-repositories*" OR Processes.process="*/tmp/*" OR Processes.process="*/dev/tcp*") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where NOT match(process, "git-lfs|git-shell|git rev-list|git pack-objects")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name=gitea OR Processes.parent_process_name=git) (Processes.process_name=bash OR Processes.process_name=sh OR Processes.process_name=dash OR Processes.process_name=python OR Processes.process_name=python3 OR Processes.process_name=perl OR Processes.process_name=nc OR Processes.process_name=ncat OR Processes.process_name=curl OR Processes.process_name=wget) (Processes.process="*hooks/*" OR Processes.process="*gitea-repositories*" OR Processes.process="*/tmp/*" OR Processes.process="*/dev/tcp*") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where NOT match(process, "git-lfs|git-shell|git rev-list|git pack-objects")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-59774", "CVE-2026-60004", "CVE-2026-20896", "CVE-2026-27771")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-59774", "CVE-2026-60004", "CVE-2026-20896", "CVE-2026-27771")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
