| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name IN ("update.bin","Client.dll") AND (Filesystem.file_path IN ("*\\AppData\\*","*\\Temp\\*","*\\Public\\*","*\\Downloads\\*")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | sort - lastTime
FDMTP backdoor C2 beacon to icloud-cdn.net AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound connections to icloud-cdn.net, the FDMTP command-and-control / defense-evasion domain used by the deployed backdoor to receive GetInfo requests, plugins and commands and to exfiltrate the host survey. Anchors on the second-source-confirmed C2 IOC, surfacing the initiating (side-loaded host) process. Rationale: icloud-cdn.net is the pre-extracted C2/defense-evasion IOC tied to FDMTP beaconing and exfiltration; a typosquat of Apple's iCloud CDN, it has no legitimate enterprise use. Surfacing InitiatingProcessSHA256 exposes the side-loaded host process. Cross-checked against: • https://www.darktrace.com/blog/chinese-apt-campaign-targets-entities-with-updated-fdmtp-backdoor • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.fdmtp
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Typo-driven user browsing to a parked/unrelated icloud-cdn.net page
  • Threat-intel/IOC validation tooling resolving the domain
  • Sandbox detonation traffic
  • Protective-DNS logging the blocked query
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess and its SHA256 — a side-loaded/non-browser process beaconing to icloud-cdn.net is high-confidence FDMTP. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block icloud-cdn.net and cdns3.51quickfox.cn, and kill/quarantine the beaconing binary and its side-loaded Client.dll/update.bin. 3) Hunt: review scheduled task creation and Run-key writes by the same host process (FDMTP plugin persistence) and check for outbound host-survey uploads following a GetInfo exchange.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "icloud-cdn.net" or RemoteUrl endswith ".icloud-cdn.net"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Beacons=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,5) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Beacons desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "icloud-cdn.net"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Beacons=count() by SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, DnsQuery
| order by Beacons desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

ChainDrop supply chain compromise: Anatomy of a self-propagating worm

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-08-04 16 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A credential-stealing worm hidden in more than 400 compromised npm packages automatically spread across software ecosystems by republishing malicious updates. This analysis details the attack chain, affected environments, and practical guidance for detection, hunting, and remediation. npm preinstall lifecycle hook launching 'node setup.mjs' (ChainDrop/Shai-Hulud loader) AIInstallation High
Hunts the ChainDrop worm's execution primitive: a compromised npm package whose preinstall hook launches the embedded setup.mjs loader via node. This is the exact string ('node setup.mjs') published by Microsoft Threat Intelligence and is the earliest on-host signal of an affected package install. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim 'node setup.mjs' invocation and the npm preinstall parent context published by Microsoft; corroborated by StepSecurity and Zscaler analyses of the same setup.mjs loader. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/a-mini-shai-hulud-has-appeared • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/shai-hulud-v2-poses-risk-npm-supply-chain
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal package whose author happens to ship a benign setup.mjs run at preinstall
  • Monorepo bootstrap scripts that call a locally-named setup.mjs
  • Developer running a hand-written build helper named setup.mjs from a project root
  • CI base-image provisioning that legitimately shells node against a setup.mjs
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("run build","run bootstrap") and FolderPath has_any (@"\corp-internal\", @"\company-monorepo\"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: On the alerting host/runner, pull the full parent chain and the package/tarball being installed (InitiatingProcessCommandLine) and hash setup.mjs against the article IOCs (54dc7ea5..., fd3ca400...). Confirm whether it was an npm/yarn/pnpm install. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the workstation/build runner and immediately revoke+rotate every credential reachable from that identity (npm publish token, GitHub PAT/OIDC, AWS keys, Vault, kube) from a known-clean host. 3) HUNT: Pivot to bun execution (UC2), outbound to npm-cache.com (UC4), IMDS reads (UC6), and any npm publish originating from this host (UC7).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("node","node.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm","npm.cmd","node","node.exe","yarn","pnpm","bun","bun.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("preinstall","npm install","npm ci","npm-cli.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","node","yarn","pnpm","bun") or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("preinstall","npm install","npm ci")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

setup.mjs spawning Bun runtime to execute obfuscated payload from node_modules/bun-dl AIInstallation High
Hunts stage-2 of ChainDrop: the setup.mjs loader launching the Bun runtime to run the heavily-obfuscated ~728KB Math_*.js credential-stealer, executing from a node_modules path or a 'bun-dl-' download directory. Bun as a child of a node/setup.mjs install context is highly abnormal. Rationale: Uses the article's Block-2 pivot (bun child of node setup.mjs, bun-dl- folder, node_modules) plus the corroborated Math_*.js payload name; Bun in an npm-install process tree is a rare, high-fidelity artifact of this specific worm. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/a-mini-shai-hulud-has-appeared
ATT&CKT1027 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Teams that legitimately use Bun as their JS runtime/bundler in local dev
  • CI pipelines that install Bun via a bun-dl style downloader for legitimate builds
  • A developer manually testing a Bun script located under node_modules
  • Bun-based test runners invoked by a project's own tooling
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code.exe","bun.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun test","bun run dev") and not (ProcessCommandLine has "Math_"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the Bun binary path and hash; check whether the org uses Bun at all and whether the parent was setup.mjs. Grab the payload path (Math_*.js) and hash it. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host/runner; treat all identity material as exposed and rotate from clean infra. 3) HUNT: Look for outbound to oven-sh/bun releases (bun download), C2 to npm-cache.com/pypi-get.com (UC4), and IMDS/credential enumeration (UC6) on the same host within minutes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs"
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("node_modules","Math_",".js")
   or FolderPath contains "bun-dl-"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "bun"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs" or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node_modules","bun-dl-","Math_")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChainDrop known-bad file drop: setup.mjs / Math_*.js hashes on disk AIInstallation Medium
Signature-grade detection on the three Microsoft-published SHA256 hashes for the ChainDrop setup.mjs loaders and the Math_*.js payload landing on a workstation or build runner. Deterministic confirmation an affected tarball was unpacked/executed. Rationale: Pure IOC match on the three Microsoft-published ChainDrop SHA256 values (setup.mjs loader variants + Math_*.js); zero interpretation risk and confirmed in the article's IOC table. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/

  • EDR/AV quarantine copy of the file re-hashing on a scanning host

| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-lab","ir-analysis") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MpCmdRun.exe"))

ChainDrop C2 exfiltration from node/bun to npm-cache.com / pypi-get.com / js-mirror.com AICommand & Control High
Detects the encrypted exfiltration channel: node or bun contacting the ChainDrop attacker-controlled HTTPS endpoints (npm-cache.com, pypi-get.com, js-mirror.com) to POST AES-256-GCM/RSA-OAEP encrypted credential bundles. Process-scoped to the worm runtimes to keep it high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the three exfil C2 domains from the article's pre-extracted IOCs and IOC table, scoped to the node/bun runtimes that actually perform exfiltration; npm-cache.com is independently confirmed as the HTTPS fallback endpoint by hackread/Wiz. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/ • https://hackread.com/shai-hulud-npm-worm-poisoning-1280-packages/

  • Threat-intel enrichment services resolving the IOC domains for reputation checks
  • DNS sinkhole/passive-DNS collectors resolving the domain for logging
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-lab","threatintel"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the resolving/connecting process is node/bun and the source is a real dev/CI host; capture bytes-out and destination. 2) CONTAIN: Block the three domains at proxy/DNS, isolate the host, and rotate every credential reachable from that identity (npm, GitHub, AWS, Vault, kube) from clean infra — assume exfiltration succeeded. 3) HUNT: Check for GitHub fallback exfil (new public repo described 'Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again', results-<timestamp>-<counter>.json commits), IMDS reads (UC6), and republish activity (UC7).

ChainDrop IMDS credential theft: node/bun reading cloud instance metadata (169.254.169.254 / 169.254.170.2) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the ChainDrop credential-enumeration behaviour where the Bun/node payload calls cloud instance-metadata endpoints to steal AWS/ECS role credentials on build runners. A JS runtime hitting link-local IMDS is highly abnormal outside SDK-driven app code and is a strong signal on a compromised runner. Rationale: The article describes AWS/Kubernetes/Vault credential enumeration via API calls; second sources (Wiz/hackread) explicitly list IMDS reads from 169.254.169.254 and 169.254.170.2 by build agents as a ChainDrop IOC. Scoping to node/bun cuts SDK/app-driven metadata noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/ • https://hackread.com/shai-hulud-npm-worm-poisoning-1280-packages/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1552.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Node.js app on an EC2/ECS host using the AWS SDK, which reads IMDS for role credentials
  • CI runner tooling written in Bun that legitimately queries ECS task metadata (169.254.170.2)
  • Health/monitoring agents embedded in a node service polling instance metadata
  • aws-sdk-js credential provider chain doing routine IMDSv2 token fetches
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","node_modules","preinstall") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm","node.exe","bun.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine if the node/bun process is a legitimate long-running app (SDK) or an install-time process spawned from setup.mjs/npm. Correlate timing with a package install and UC1/UC2 hits. 2) CONTAIN: If tied to install, isolate the runner and immediately rotate the instance/role credentials and any Vault/kube secrets reachable; disable the affected role's active sessions. 3) HUNT: Trace what the stolen role could reach (S3, secrets manager, CloudTrail AssumeRole), and check for exfil (UC4) and republish (UC7).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","bun","bun.exe")
| where RemoteIP in ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2")
| where SrcUsername != "" or isnotempty(SrcHostname)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChainDrop persistence: node/bun injecting .claude and .vscode config files into repositories AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the ChainDrop persistence and developer-to-developer spread mechanism where the payload writes malicious Claude (.claude/) and Visual Studio Code (.vscode/) configuration files into local repositories. Scoped to writes performed by the node/bun worm runtimes to separate from normal IDE activity. Rationale: Directly targets the article's stated persistence/spread routine (inject .claude and .vscode config files via the loader hash fd3ca400...), constrained to node/bun writers driven by setup.mjs to reduce normal IDE churn. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/ • https://www.upwind.io/feed/shai-hulud-2-npm-supply-chain-worm-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • VS Code or an extension legitimately writing .vscode/settings.json during project setup
  • A dev tool scaffolding a .claude/ config as part of normal onboarding
  • postinstall scripts of legitimate packages that write editor config
  • A formatter/linter run via node updating .vscode config
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("code.exe","Code.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("eslint","prettier","scaffold"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the written .claude/.vscode files for injected commands/hooks and confirm the writer was a setup.mjs/npm-install context, not the user's IDE. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, remove the injected config across all repo branches, and rotate GitHub credentials/tokens used by the identity. 3) HUNT: Check git history for pushed .claude/.vscode changes from this identity, and pivot to any repos the token could write to.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.claude\", "/.claude/", @"\.vscode\", "/.vscode/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","bun","bun.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","node_modules","Math_") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm","node.exe","bun.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/.claude/", "\\.claude\\", "/.vscode/", "\\.vscode\\")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","bun")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","node_modules","Math_")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ChainDrop .claude and .vscode config injection by node or bun
id: 4f7b2c19-8d3e-4a05-9b62-6c1e3a2d7f06
description: Detects the ChainDrop worm runtime writing malicious .claude and .vscode configuration files into repositories for persistence and developer-to-developer spread

ChainDrop worm propagation: npm publish spawned from a package-install context AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the self-propagation routine where the ChainDrop payload uses a stolen npm token to republish tarballs: an 'npm publish' (or programmatic publish) invoked as a child of the node/bun worm runtime or from within node_modules, rather than an interactive developer release. This is the mechanism turning one compromised identity into hundreds of malicious releases. Rationale: Targets the article's core propagation routine ('After obtaining an npm publishing token... republishes the modified packages'): a publish command parented by the worm runtime / originating from node_modules rather than an interactive dev shell. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate CI release pipeline running 'npm publish' from a node-based release script
  • semantic-release / np / changesets tooling publishing programmatically via node
  • A developer publishing from a monorepo where the script runs under node_modules tooling
  • Internal automation republishing scoped packages to a private registry
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("semantic-release","changeset","np ") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","Math_")))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm whether this publish belongs to a sanctioned release pipeline; check the parent chain for setup.mjs/bun and whether it ran on a dev workstation vs. release runner. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the npm publishing token immediately and place a publish hold; isolate the host. Check npm for versions published by this identity with no matching git commit/tag. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every package the token could publish, diff recently-published versions for injected preinstall/setup.mjs, and notify the registry to yank malicious versions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FileName in~ ("npm","npm.cmd") and ProcessCommandLine has "publish")
     or (FileName in~ ("node","node.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("npm","publish"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","bun","bun.exe")
     or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","node_modules","Math_")
     or ProcessCommandLine has "node_modules"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "publish" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "npm"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","bun") or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","node_modules") or ActingProcessCommandLine has "node_modules"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ChainDrop worm npm publish from install context
id: 9a4d6e33-5c71-4b28-8f09-2d7b1c6a3f07
description: Detects an npm publish invoked as a child of the node/bun worm runtime or from within node_modules, characteristic of ChainDrop self-propagation
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/05
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1195.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'npm'
      - 'publish'
  selection_ctx:
    - ParentImage|endswith:
        - '/node'
        - '\node.exe'
        - '/bun'
        - '\bun.exe'
    - ParentCommandLine|contains: 'setup.mjs'
    - CommandLine|contains: 'node_modules'
  condition: selection_cmd and selection_ctx
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:(*npm*publish* OR *"npm publish"*) (@ParentImage:(*\node.exe OR *\bun.exe OR *\NODE.EXE OR *\BUN.EXE) OR @ParentCommandLine:*setup.mjs* OR @CommandLine:*node_modules*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| regex("npm.*publish", field=CommandLine)
| ParentBaseFileName=/(node|bun)(\.exe)?$/i OR regex("setup\.mjs|node_modules", field=ParentCommandLine) OR regex("node_modules", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*publish*" AND (Processes.process="*npm*" OR Processes.process_name IN ("npm","npm.cmd","node","node.exe"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where parent_process_name IN ("node","node.exe","bun","bun.exe") OR like(parent_process, "%setup.mjs%") OR like(parent_process, "%node_modules%") OR like(process, "%node_modules%")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*publish*" AND (Processes.process="*npm*" OR Processes.process_name IN ("npm","npm.cmd","node","node.exe"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where parent_process_name IN ("node","node.exe","bun","bun.exe") OR like(parent_process, "%setup.mjs%") OR like(parent_process, "%node_modules%") OR like(process, "%node_modules%")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"

| where Account !endswith "$"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: |

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1204.002

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:

            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

            - 'invoke-expression'

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Rogue device adoption from the public internet to Omada controller (default-cred/race exploit) · [LLM] Stored XSS / JavaScript injection into Omada controller admin UI (CVE-2025-9289) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Internet-sourced enumeration of TP-Link Omada device-adoption ports (29810-29816) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts external hosts probing an internet-exposed Omada controller's zero-touch-provisioning port range (29810 discovery through 29816 rtty). Forescout found 1,800+ controllers reachable this way; these ports are intended for on-LAN device adoption only, so public-internet volume against them is the serial-number/MAC enumeration step of the ZTP attack chain. Rationale: Pivots on the exact Omada ZTP port range (29810 discovery, 29811 manager.v1, 29812 adopt.v1, 29813 upgrade.v1, 29814 manager.v2, 29815 transfer.v2, 29816 rtty) confirmed against TP-Link's own port FAQ, combined with an external-source predicate — this is the concrete shape of the serial/MAC enumeration Forescout described. Cross-checked TP-Link/Omada advisory and port documentation. Cross-checked against: • https://support.omadanetworks.com/us/bulletin/114950/ • https://support.omadanetworks.com/us/document/13087/ • https://www.tp-link.com/us/support/faq/3281/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/10/tp-link-patches-four-omada-gateway.html
ATT&CKT1595.001 T1595.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internet-wide background scanners (Shodan, Censys, GreyNoise) sweeping the 29810-29816 range against an accidentally-exposed controller
  • A legitimate remote MSP performing bulk device adoption over a site-to-site VPN whose egress IP is not in the RFC1918 exclusion list
  • NAT/CGNAT collapsing many internal adoption sessions behind one public IP, inflating the per-source count
  • Security team's own external vulnerability scanner (Qualys/Nessus/Forescout) profiling the controller
  • Load-balancer or reverse-proxy health checks hitting the management ports
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<known_scanner_ips_ref_table>"]))     // replace with a watchlist(); optional GreyNoise/known-scanner suppression
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the DestinationIP is an Omada controller and whether it is intentionally internet-exposed; check whether the SourceIP is a known scanner (GreyNoise) or a single actor touching multiple adoption ports. 2) Contain: if the controller should not be internet-facing, firewall-block inbound WAN to 29810-29816 (and 8043/8088/8843) immediately and restrict adoption to the management VLAN. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same SourceIP for follow-on allowed connections to the adoption port (see the initial-access UC), and review the controller for any device adopted from an external address or duplicate serial/MAC.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where RemotePort between (29810 .. 29816)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where RemoteIPType == "Private"
| summarize Conns=count(), DistinctPorts=dcount(RemotePort), DestPorts=make_set(RemotePort), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP
| where Conns > 20     // 20 = enumeration threshold; a legit host adopts a device with a handful of packets, not a sweep
| order by Conns desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DestinationPort between (29810 .. 29816)
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false     // adoption/discovery must originate on-LAN; public source = probing an exposed controller
| summarize Conns=count(), DistinctPorts=dcount(DestinationPort), DestPorts=make_set(DestinationPort), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DestinationIP
| where Conns > 20     // 20 = enumeration threshold vs. background single-packet internet scans
| order by Conns desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort>=29810 RemotePort<=29816
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=count(as=connCount))
| connCount > 20

Rogue device adoption from the public internet to Omada controller (default-cred/race exploit) AIExploitation Medium
Detects a successful/allowed inbound connection from a non-RFC1918 source to the Omada adoption ports (29812 adopt.v1 / 29814 manager.v2). Legitimate zero-touch adoption always originates from a managed device on the LAN — an allowed adoption handshake sourced from the internet is the device-spoofing + cloud-adoption race condition that lets an attacker authenticate with default credentials (CVE-2025-9290 / CVE-2025-15544 / CVE-2025-15627). Rationale: Anchors on port 29812 (port.adopt.v1) and 29814 (port.manager.v2) with an allowed action from a public source — the exact network signature of Forescout's spoof-a-pending-device + win-the-adoption-race scenario, which is impossible for a legitimately on-LAN device. Ports verified against TP-Link's Omada SDN port FAQ. Defender/Falcon left empty: the controller is a network appliance, not an EDR-onboarded endpoint, so this inbound-to-appliance flow is only visible to the perimeter firewall. Cross-checked against: • https://support.omadanetworks.com/us/bulletin/114950/ • https://www.tp-link.com/us/support/faq/3281/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-9289/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cloud-based/off-site Omada controller legitimately adopting remote devices over WAN where those devices' public IPs are expected
  • Remote branch device adopting through a controller whose firewall NATs the branch to a public IP not in the RFC1918 list
  • A misconfigured firewall rule that legitimately forwards WAN traffic to adoption ports for a supported remote-adoption deployment
  • Penetration test or Forescout/BAS tooling replaying the adoption exploit against the controller
Suppression filter
| where DestinationIP !in (dynamic(["<sanctioned_wan_adoption_controller_ips>"]))     // optional: exclude controllers with an approved remote-adoption deployment (watchlist)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the SourceIP geolocation/ASN and whether any remote-adoption deployment is sanctioned; on the controller, list devices adopted in the alert window and look for a device whose serial/MAC was already present (duplicate/spoof) or that used default credentials. 2) Contain: block inbound WAN to 29812/29814 at the firewall, force-remove the rogue device, and rotate the controller admin password plus any exposed device secrets (cleartext username, MD5 hash, VPN keys). 3) Hunt: from the same SourceIP look for a preceding enumeration burst and subsequent XSS payloads to the admin ports (8043/8088/8843), and audit for newly created VPN tunnels or config pushes.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DestinationPort in (29812, 29814)     // port.adopt.v1 / port.manager.v2 — the device-adoption handshake
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false     // adoption from the internet should never happen; it is a spoofed/rogue device
| where DeviceAction in~ ("allow","allowed","permit","accept","Permit")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceAction, SentBytes, ReceivedBytes, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Stored XSS / JavaScript injection into Omada controller admin UI (CVE-2025-9289) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests to the Omada controller web-admin ports (8043/8088/8843) carrying JavaScript/HTML injection markers. Maps CVE-2025-9289 and CVE-2025-15628 — the attacker persists script in an admin field so an authenticated administrator's browser executes it and phishes their cloud-controller credentials. Rationale: Combines the Omada web-admin ports (8043/8088/8843, per TP-Link's port FAQ) with common XSS injection tokens to catch the CVE-2025-9289/CVE-2025-15628 admin-UI JavaScript injection Forescout used to phish admin credentials. URL/query-based payloads are captured; note stored-XSS via POST body may be missed if the proxy does not log bodies — pair with the ImWebSession table where request bodies are available. Defender/Falcon empty: web request targets the appliance, not an EDR host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-9289/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-9289 • https://support.omadanetworks.com/us/bulletin/114950/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1189
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security scanner (Burp/ZAP/Qualys) actively testing the controller for XSS with the same payload tokens
  • A legitimate admin pasting configuration text that happens to contain 'onload=' or 'javascript:' into a controller field
  • URL-encoded query strings in normal portal-authentication flows that coincidentally contain matched substrings
  • WAF logging both the request and its own sanitized copy, double-counting the event
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Burp", "Nessus", "Qualys", "OWASP ZAP", "nuclei")     // suppress known security-scanner user-agents
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the RequestMethod/RequestURL contains an actual injection (decode %3Cscript) versus a scanner probe, and identify whether the SourceIP is internal (admin browser) or external; capture the DestinationIP controller. 2) Contain: if a persisted payload is confirmed, restrict admin-UI access to a management VLAN, patch to the fixed Omada firmware, and invalidate admin sessions plus rotate cloud-controller credentials. 3) Hunt: correlate the SourceIP with prior adoption-port activity, and review controller admin fields/objects for stored script and any anomalous outbound POST of admin credentials to attacker infrastructure.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DestinationPort in (8043, 8088, 8843)     // Omada controller web-admin/portal ports
| where RequestURL has_any ("<script", "javascript:", "onerror=", "onload=", "%3Cscript", "document.cookie", "String.fromCharCode")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

DeviceProcessEvents

let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
