Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Spoofed RingCentral email delivered to inbox despite SPF/DMARC failure (whitelist abuse) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Microsoft 365 device-code authorization grant redeemed (Greatness device-code phishing) · [LLM] Endpoint/proxy connections to Greatness AiTM phishing infrastructure · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] M365 token replay / sign-in from Greatness IOC IP and VPS/VPN hosting ASNs · [LLM] Bulk Microsoft Graph / M365 workload enumeration in a single session (post-compromise discovery) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Spoofed RingCentral email delivered to inbox despite SPF/DMARC failure (whitelist abuse) AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound mail whose header From claims ringcentral.com (service@ringcentral.com) but which fails SPF/DMARC and carries no DKIM, yet still lands in the inbox because RingCentral was safe-listed. This is the exact whitelist-abuse delivery vector the Greatness operators used to bypass Exchange filtering (SCL -1). Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact spoofed sender (service@ringcentral.com), the header-vs-envelope mismatch (IONOS origin, not ringcentral.com), the SPF/DMARC failure with no DKIM, and inbox delivery — the precise combination that produced SCL -1. Very few legitimate RingCentral notifications fail all auth checks yet reach the inbox. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://www.techradar.com/pro/security/microsoft-365-users-hit-by-phishing-scheme-posing-as-ringcentral-emails
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656 T1114.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate RingCentral notifications relayed through a third-party sending service that breaks SPF alignment
  • Internal mail-forwarding rules that strip DKIM and cause DMARC to fail on genuine RingCentral mail
  • Marketing/ESP platforms sending on RingCentral's behalf from a non-aligned envelope domain
  • A misconfigured connector re-writing the P1/P2 sender during transport
Suppression filter
| where SenderIPv4 != "" and Auth !has "compauth: pass"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full AuthenticationDetails and SenderIPv4 for the NetworkMessageId; confirm the envelope domain is not RingCentral and the sending IP is IONOS/hosting, not RingCentral's published SPF ranges. 2) Contain: soft-delete/quarantine the message tenant-wide via EmailPostDeliveryEvents/ZAP, and remove the blanket ringcentral.com safe-sender/allow entry, replacing it with an auth-required rule. 3) Hunt: search UrlClickEvents for recipients who clicked the embedded link and pivot to sign-ins from the Greatness IOC IP 38.248.95.214 and domains aitomayu.com / panel.securehubcloud.com.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderFromDomain =~ "ringcentral.com" or SenderFromAddress =~ "service@ringcentral.com" or SenderDisplayName has "RingCentral"
// header From claims RingCentral but envelope/auth does not match (IONOS-origin, no DKIM)
| where SenderMailFromDomain !~ "ringcentral.com"
| where DeliveryAction == "Delivered" and DeliveryLocation == "Inbox"
| extend Auth = tostring(AuthenticationDetails)
| where Auth has "fail" or Auth has "softfail" or Auth has "none"   // SPF/DMARC fail or DKIM none
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, SenderIPv4, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderFromDomain =~ "ringcentral.com" or SenderFromAddress =~ "service@ringcentral.com" or SenderDisplayName has "RingCentral"
// header From claims RingCentral but envelope/auth does not match (IONOS-origin, no DKIM)
| where SenderMailFromDomain !~ "ringcentral.com"
| where DeliveryAction == "Delivered" and DeliveryLocation == "Inbox"
| extend Auth = tostring(AuthenticationDetails)
| where Auth has "fail" or Auth has "softfail" or Auth has "none"   // SPF/DMARC fail or DKIM none
| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, SenderIPv4, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Microsoft 365 device-code authorization grant redeemed (Greatness device-code phishing) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts successful, non-interactive device-code authentication grants against Microsoft 365 — the second capture path Greatness added alongside AiTM. Device-code phishing tricks a victim into approving an OAuth device authorization code, handing the attacker a token without any credential prompt on attacker infrastructure. Rationale: The article explicitly names a 'device-code phishing flow' as one of two Greatness capture paths; corroborated by The Hacker News. Device-code grants are rare in most tenants, so successful redemptions are a high-value hunt, especially when the redeeming IP is a hosting/VPN provider (pivot with UC3). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phishing-service-spoofs-ringcentral-to-steal-microsoft-365-accounts/
ATT&CKT1528 T1621
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code sign-ins from CLI tools (Azure CLI, az login --use-device-code) by developers/admins
  • Onboarding of shared/kiosk devices or smart-TV/conference-room apps that use device authorization grant
  • PowerShell/Graph SDK automation authenticating via device code on headless hosts
  • IoT or input-constrained device enrollment that legitimately uses the device-code flow
Suppression filter
| where not(AppDisplayName in~ ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell") and IsInteractive == false)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the AccountUpn normally uses device-code auth and whether the IPAddress is a residential ISP or hosting/VPN provider; inspect ResourceDisplayName (Graph/Exchange). 2) Contain: if unexpected, revoke the user's refresh/access tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force password reset, and re-require MFA. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same AccountUpn for subsequent Graph enumeration (UC4) and token replay from hosting IPs (UC3); block device-code flow via Conditional Access if not needed operationally.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" or AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "deviceCode"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, ClientAppUsed, IsInteractive, ConditionalAccessStatus, UserAgent
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, AutonomousSystemNumber, ClientAppUsed, IsInteractive, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
M365 token replay / sign-in from Greatness IOC IP and VPS/VPN hosting ASNs AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts successful Microsoft 365 sign-ins and non-interactive token redemptions originating from the campaign's IOC IP (38.248.95.214) and from commercial VPS/VPN autonomous systems. Post-compromise, Greatness operators replayed AiTM-captured, MFA-approved tokens from VPS and commercial VPN infrastructure to reach mailboxes and Graph. Rationale: 38.248.95.214 is a named IOC in the article; the VPS/VPN ASN list operationalises the article's statement that tokens were 'replayed from VPS and commercial VPN infrastructure.' Non-interactive successful access to Graph/Exchange from these sources is a strong post-AiTM replay signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phishing-service-spoofs-ringcentral-to-steal-microsoft-365-accounts/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1539
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate VPN egress or cloud-hosted VDI/jump hosts that legitimately place user sign-ins in hosting ASNs
  • Sanctioned SaaS integrations or backup tools accessing Exchange/SharePoint from cloud IPs
  • Security scanners / mailbox migration tooling running from AWS/Azure
  • Traveling users on commercial VPN apps (may overlap with hosting ASNs)
Suppression filter
| where not(UserAgent has_any ("Veeam","CloudMigration","Backup") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: for hits, confirm the AccountUpn's normal IP/geo and whether the session is non-interactive token use; the exact IOC IP 38.248.95.214 is auto-confirm. 2) Contain: revoke all refresh/access tokens, reset credentials, and disable the account if replay is confirmed; add the IP/ASN to Conditional Access block. 3) Hunt: correlate with the AiTM infra visit (UC5) and device-code grants (UC2), and enumerate what the session touched via Graph enumeration (UC4).
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where IPAddress == "38.248.95.214"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country, City, Application, ResourceDisplayName, IsInteractive, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, ConditionalAccessStatus
| order by Timestamp desc
// Commercial hosting / VPS ASNs commonly used for token replay (Linode, DigitalOcean, OVH, AWS, Azure, Google, Vultr, Hetzner, Contabo, M247)
let HostingASNs = dynamic([63949,14061,16276,14618,16509,8075,15169,20473,24940,51167,9009]);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where IPAddress == "38.248.95.214" or AutonomousSystemNumber in (HostingASNs)
| where ResourceDisplayName has_any ("Microsoft Graph","Office 365 Exchange Online","Office 365 SharePoint Online")
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AutonomousSystemNumber, Location, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IsInteractive, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @network.client.ip:38.248.95.214
Bulk Microsoft Graph / M365 workload enumeration in a single session (post-compromise discovery) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a single account fanning out across Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams within a short window — the mailbox/Teams/SharePoint/OneDrive/contacts/calendar/registered-app enumeration Greatness operators performed via Microsoft Graph, with access persisting for over two weeks. Rationale: Directly models the article's enumeration list (Outlook mailboxes, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, contacts, calendars, registered apps) as a cross-workload fan-out in one session, with the IOC IP flagged as a confidence booster. Legitimate users rarely touch 4 distinct workloads in a single hour from one session. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phishing-service-spoofs-ringcentral-to-steal-microsoft-365-accounts/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html
ATT&CKT1526 T1213 T1087.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power users or executives who genuinely work across Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive in a busy hour
  • eDiscovery, compliance or DLP tooling that reads across all workloads
  • Newly onboarded users whose clients sync every workload at once
  • Mailbox/SharePoint migration or backup jobs enumerating content
Suppression filter
| where not(AccountDisplayName has_any ("eDiscovery","Compliance","Migration","Backup"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the account's session originates from a hosting/VPN IP (HasGreatnessIP == true is auto-escalate) and whether the fan-out is human-paced or programmatic. 2) Contain: revoke tokens and reset credentials for the account; review and revoke suspicious OAuth app consents and registered applications. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same AccountObjectId to token replay (UC3), device-code grants (UC2) and AiTM infra visits (UC5); check for new inbox rules or forwarding.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where Application in ("Microsoft Graph","Microsoft Exchange Online","Microsoft SharePoint Online","Microsoft OneDrive for Business","Microsoft Teams")
| where isnotempty(AccountObjectId) and AccountType == "Regular"
| summarize Workloads = dcount(Application), AppSet = make_set(Application), ActionSet = make_set(ActionType, 30), Events = count(), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), ISPs = make_set(ISP, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where Workloads >= 4   // Exchange + SharePoint + OneDrive + Teams touched within 1h = Graph recon fan-out
| extend HasGreatnessIP = IPs has "38.248.95.214"
| order by Workloads desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Operation in ("MailItemsAccessed","FileAccessed","FileDownloaded","FilePreviewed","SharePointFileOperation","SearchQueryPerformed")
| summarize Workloads = dcount(OfficeWorkload), WorkloadSet = make_set(OfficeWorkload), Ops = make_set(Operation, 30), Events = count(), IPs = make_set(ClientIP, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by UserId, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Workloads >= 3   // multiple M365 workloads enumerated in one hour by one account
| extend HasGreatnessIP = IPs has "38.248.95.214"
| order by Workloads desc
Endpoint/proxy connections to Greatness AiTM phishing infrastructure AIExploitation High
Hunts hosts resolving or connecting to the Greatness AiTM/reverse-proxy infrastructure — aitomayu.com, panel.securehubcloud.com, and 38.248.95.214 — which sits between the victim and login.microsoftonline.com to capture MFA-approved tokens after the RingCentral lure is clicked. Rationale: aitomayu.com, panel.securehubcloud.com and 38.248.95.214 are named IOCs; any org host contacting them is a direct hit on Greatness AiTM/panel infrastructure. Case-insensitive matching and the securehubcloud.com wildcard catch subdomain variants of the reverse-proxy panel. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phishing-service-spoofs-ringcentral-to-steal-microsoft-365-accounts/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html
ATT&CKT1557 T1539 T1566.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers or SOC analysts deliberately detonating the phishing URL in a sandbox
  • Threat-intel/URL-scanning services resolving the domains from corporate egress
  • Sinkholed or newly re-registered domain resolving to benign parked infrastructure
  • Proxy pre-fetch/link-rewrite services (Safe Links) touching the URL on the user's behalf

| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("sandbox","detonation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the DeviceName/SourceUserName and confirm the connection was user-driven (browser process) versus a scanner; the exact IOC IP/domains are auto-confirm. 2) Contain: block aitomayu.com, panel.securehubcloud.com and 38.248.95.214 at proxy/firewall/DNS, isolate the host if a browser session reached the AiTM proxy, and revoke the user's M365 tokens. 3) Hunt: for any user who reached the infra, check for successful M365 sign-ins from hosting IPs (UC3), device-code grants (UC2) and Graph enumeration (UC4); review inbox rules and OAuth consents.
DeviceNetworkEvents

| order by Timestamp desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent

| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")

        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ChainDrop npm Worm: Bun-loaded CI/CD credential harvester with Ethereum dead-dro
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Unauthenticated Flowise OAuth2 token-refresh endpoint access from external source (CVE-2026-70478) AIExploitation High
Hunts external/public source IPs POSTing to the whitelisted, no-auth Flowise endpoint /api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/:credentialId and receiving HTTP 200, which returns the connected-service access_token in the body. Article-specific to the exact vulnerable route and its successful-response shape. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable route '/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/' with POST + HTTP 200 (the article states a valid ID returns the new access_token in the body, while unknown IDs return 'Credential not found'). External source filter (ipv4_is_private) removes the app's own frontend, which is the legitimate caller. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty: no web-access-log table exists in Defender XDR (DeviceNetworkEvents lacks URL path), FDR ships no HTTP path, and this is not AWS-native telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/flowise/CVE-2026-70478/ • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-70478 • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/flowise-unauthenticated-oauth-secrets-disclosure-via-api-v1-loginmethod-endpoint
ATT&CKT1190 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Azure App Service platform health-check probes hitting the app root (filter by UserAgent)
  • Legitimate Flowise UI running on a public IP not covered by RFC1918 (SaaS/cloud-hosted analyst workstation)
  • Reverse proxy that rewrites CIp to the proxy's own address, masking true client and collapsing all traffic to one IP
  • Security scanner / ASM tooling authorised to probe the app
  • Load balancer synthetic monitoring calling the API
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "AlwaysOn" and UserAgent !has "HealthCheck" and UserAgent !has "Edge Health Probe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all rows for the offending CIp — confirm the source is outside your management/VPN ranges and that ScStatus==200 (token actually returned). Extract the credentialId values from CsUriStem. 2) Contain: patch Flowise to >=3.1.3 immediately (removes endpoint from WHITELIST_URLS); block the source IP at the WAF; for each exposed credentialId, revoke and rotate the linked OAuth client secret and refresh token at the provider (Google/Microsoft/GitHub). 3) Hunt: search connected-service sign-in logs (SigninLogs/CloudAppEvents) for use of the stolen access tokens from attacker infrastructure, and check for enumeration/burst patterns from the same IP (companion UCs).
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where CsMethod == "POST"
| where CsUriStem has "/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/"
| where ScStatus == 200
| where not(ipv4_is_private(CIp))
| summarize Requests = count(), DistinctCredIds = dcount(CsUriStem), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5) by CIp, CsHost
| order by Requests desc

Flowise OAuth2 credentialId enumeration (mixed 200/404 probing) AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects a single source probing many distinct credentialId values against the unauthenticated Flowise refresh endpoint within a short window, with a mix of HTTP 200 (valid IDs) and 404/403 (misses) — the discovery step the attacker uses to find live credential IDs before token theft. Rationale: Article's Docker validation shows unknown IDs return 'Credential not found' (a 4xx) while valid IDs succeed, so a burst of distinct credentialId path values with a 200/miss mix on this exact route is the enumeration fingerprint. 5-in-2-minutes threshold separates scanning from a user's single-credential UI refresh. Aggregation/threshold logic so no Sigma; not Defender/FDR/AWS telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/flowise/CVE-2026-70478/ • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-70478
ATT&CKT1595.003 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An admin bulk-refreshing many stored credentials from the Flowise UI in a maintenance window
  • Automated internal job that iterates credentials to keep tokens warm
  • Broken frontend retry loop hammering the endpoint with the same/few IDs (would show low distinct-ID count — tune threshold)
  • Web vulnerability scanner authorised against the app generating 404s across guessed paths
  • CDN/proxy collapsing multiple real users to one egress IP
Suppression filter
| where CIp !in (dynamic([]))  // populate with known maintenance/automation egress IPs after first tuning pass
Response runbook
1) Triage: list the distinct credentialId values the source requested and their status codes — a wide spread of UUIDs with 404s confirms enumeration; note which returned 200. 2) Contain: block the source IP; upgrade to Flowise >=3.1.3; rotate secrets for any credentialId that returned 200 during the burst. 3) Hunt: pivot to the burst-refresh UC for the same IP to see if enumeration was followed by mass successful token pulls, and review connected-service logs for token misuse.

| summarize Total = count(), DistinctCredIds = dcount(CsUriStem), NotFound = countif(ScStatus in (404, 403, 500)), Valid = countif(ScStatus == 200), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by CIp, bin(TimeGenerated, 2m)
| where DistinctCredIds >= 5 and NotFound >= 1   // 5+ distinct credential IDs probed in 2 min with >=1 miss = enumeration
| order by DistinctCredIds desc

Flowise mass OAuth token harvest — burst of successful refreshes across credentials AIActions on Objectives High
Detects one source obtaining HTTP 200 refreshes for 5+ distinct credential IDs within 5 minutes on the unauthenticated Flowise endpoint — the collection-phase pattern of an attacker draining every connected-service access token after finding valid IDs. Rationale: The article states the flaw 'enables token theft for any connected service' and each 200 returns a fresh access_token; harvesting all victims means many distinct credentialId successes in a tight window. Distinct-credential threshold (>=5/5min) is what separates a mass pull from routine single-credential refreshes. Threshold correlation so no Sigma; web telemetry only, hence Defender/FDR/AWS empty. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/flowise/CVE-2026-70478/ • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/flowise-unauthenticated-oauth-secrets-disclosure-via-api-v1-loginmethod-endpoint
ATT&CKT1528 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scheduled bulk token-refresh maintenance job across all stored credentials
  • Flowise instance with many active chatflows legitimately refreshing tokens near-simultaneously on expiry
  • DR/failover warm-up that re-primes all connected-service tokens
  • Load test against the Flowise API
  • Single automation account driving many credentials as designed
Suppression filter
| where CsHost !has "staging" and CsHost !has "test"
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate the distinct credentialIds successfully refreshed in the bin and the source IP(s); confirm it is not a sanctioned maintenance job. 2) Contain: block source, upgrade to Flowise >=3.1.3, and treat every credentialId in the burst as compromised — revoke/rotate each connected-service client secret and refresh token. 3) Hunt: correlate the burst timestamps with connected-service sign-in logs (SigninLogs, CloudAppEvents, GitHub/Google audit) for token use from the same or attacker-linked IPs; expand the window to catch a slow-and-low variant under threshold.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where CsMethod == "POST"

| where ScStatus == 200
| summarize SuccessfulRefreshes = count(), DistinctCredIds = dcount(CsUriStem), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Sources = make_set(CIp, 5) by CsHost, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where SuccessfulRefreshes >= 5 and DistinctCredIds >= 5   // >=5 distinct credentials refreshed in one 5-min bin = token harvest
| order by SuccessfulRefreshes desc

High-privilege OAuth consent grant to Flowise application (offline_access / Mail / Files) AIInstallation Medium
Surfaces Entra ID consent grants to the Flowise app that include offline_access or read/write mail/file scopes — these are what populate Flowise's stored refresh_tokens that CVE-2026-70478 subsequently leaks. Flags the persistence pre-condition and any newly-widened grant. Rationale: The article states stored credentials contain clientId, clientSecret and refresh_token; offline_access is exactly the scope that yields a refresh_token, and Mail/Files scopes define the blast radius of a stolen token. Scoping the grant to the 'Flowise' app name keeps it article-specific rather than a generic illicit-consent rule. Falcon/CloudWatch empty as this is Entra ID / MCAS telemetry the FDR and AWS trails do not carry; Splunk empty as no equivalent CIM AAD consent dataset is standard here. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/flowise/CVE-2026-70478/ • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/security/advisories/GHSA-6f7g-v4pp-r667
ATT&CKT1098.001 T1528
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate first-time setup of a Flowise Google/Microsoft connector by an admin (expected offline_access grant)
  • Re-consent after a scope change during normal Flowise integration expansion
  • Tenant-wide admin consent applied to Flowise as part of sanctioned onboarding
  • A differently-named but legitimate internal app containing 'Flowise' in its display name
  • Bulk consent migration during tenant restructuring
Suppression filter
| where Actor !in ("admin-onboarding@yourtenant.onmicrosoft.com")  // add sanctioned onboarding admins after baseline
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm who granted consent (Actor/AccountDisplayName), whether they are an admin, and whether the grant is expected onboarding vs. an unexpected scope widening; note the exact scopes. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, revoke the service principal's OAuth2PermissionGrants and disable the app registration; ensure the underlying Flowise deployment is patched to >=3.1.3 so stored refresh tokens can't be leaked. 3) Hunt: for each granted credential, check the web-access UCs for refresh-endpoint hits and review connected-service audit logs for token use; enumerate all apps holding offline_access + Mail/Files to find similar exposure.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.", "Add delegated permission grant.", "Add app role assignment grant to user.")
| where RawEventData has "Flowise"
| where RawEventData has_any ("offline_access", "Mail.ReadWrite", "Mail.Read", "Mail.Send", "Files.ReadWrite", "Files.Read")
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName in~ ("Consent to application", "Add delegated permission grant", "Add app role assignment grant to user")
| mv-expand TargetResources
| extend AppName = tostring(TargetResources.displayName)
| where AppName has "Flowise"
| mv-expand mp = TargetResources.modifiedProperties
| extend PropName = tostring(mp.displayName), NewVal = tostring(mp.newValue)
| where PropName has_any ("ConsentAction.Permissions", "DelegatedPermissionGrant.Scope", "AppRole.Value")
| where NewVal has_any ("offline_access", "Mail.ReadWrite", "Mail.Read", "Mail.Send", "Files.ReadWrite", "Files.Read")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, AppName, PropName, NewVal
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Flowise CSV Agent prompt-injection: validator-bypass Python tokens POSTed to /api/v1/prediction AIDelivery Medium
Hunts unauthenticated POSTs to the Flowise CSV Agent prediction endpoint whose request body carries the pyodide blocklist-bypass constructs from CVE-2026-70477 (MRO traversal, frame inspection, __import__ reconstruction). Fires on the delivery of the injection payload before code executes. Rationale: Uses the exact validator-bypass identifiers from the CVE-2026-70477 bypass table (`__subclasses__`, `__mro__`, `__build_class__`, `gi_frame`, `f_builtins`, `BuiltinImporter.load_module`, `__import__`) which are near-nonexistent in legitimate pandas DataFrame questions, plus the confirmed unauthenticated `POST /api/v1/prediction/:id` vector. Body-capture-dependent, so scoped as hunting. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/flowise-components/CVE-2026-70477/ • https://www.elttam.com/blog/cruising-for-shells-in-flowise • https://docs.flowiseai.com/using-flowise/prediction
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate data-science chatflow where a user genuinely asks a question containing the word `query` or pandas dunder attributes
  • Internal pentest / vulnerability scanner probing the Flowise instance post-patch
  • WAF that logs only headers/URI (no body) — produces false negatives, not false positives, but analysts may misread absence as clean
  • Security researcher replaying the public PoC in a sanctioned test tenant
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request body from the WAF/proxy for the flagged /api/v1/prediction hit and confirm it contains reconstructed `__import__`/`__subclasses__` chains rather than benign pandas. Note SourceIP and whether the request was authenticated. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the edge and take the Flowise instance offline or upgrade to >=3.1.3 (CSVAgent removed); if unauthenticated exposure confirmed, treat as compromised. 3) Hunt: pivot to the Flowise host EDR and check for `node`-spawned shells (UC2) and outbound connections from interpreters (UC3) within minutes of this request.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/prediction/"
| where (isempty(RequestMethod) or RequestMethod =~ "POST")
// bypass constructs live in the POST body; matched here only where the WAF forwards body content into Message / RequestURL
| where RequestURL has_any ("__subclasses__","__mro__","__build_class__","gi_frame","f_builtins","BuiltinImporter","load_module","__import__","__getattribute__")
     or Message has_any ("__subclasses__","__mro__","__build_class__","gi_frame","f_builtins","f_globals","__loader__","BuiltinImporter","load_module","__import__","__getattribute__")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, Message, DeviceProduct, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Flowise (node) process spawning a shell — CVE-2026-70477 pyodide→child_process RCE landing AIExploitation High
Detects the Flowise Node.js process spawning an OS shell, the on-host artifact of the CVE-2026-70477 CSV Agent RCE where pyodide's JS bridge reaches Node's child_process to run attacker commands. A patched, benign Flowise never shells out from the CSV Agent, making node→shell on a Flowise host high-fidelity. Rationale: Anchored on the confirmed RCE mechanism (pyodide JS bridge → Node child_process → shell) and the Flowise-specific `node ... flowise` parent command line; a legitimate CSV Agent runs pandas inside in-process WASM and never spawns an OS shell, so this is a clean true-positive signal. Datadog left empty because its auditd schema exposes no parent-process attribute to assert the `node`/`flowise` ancestry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elttam.com/blog/cruising-for-shells-in-flowise • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/flowise-components/CVE-2026-70477/ • https://docs.flowiseai.com/using-flowise/prediction
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.006 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • pm2 or other node-based process manager running a lifecycle/deploy hook that shells out
  • npm/yarn postinstall scripts executing under node spawning sh during a Flowise upgrade
  • Container entrypoint wrapper where node invokes a shell healthcheck
  • A deliberately-configured Flowise custom tool / 'Execute Flow' node that legitimately runs shell commands by design
  • Ops automation restarting the service via a node-driven wrapper
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pm2","npm","yarn","/usr/lib/node_modules/npm","HEALTHCHECK","entrypoint") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine — attacker commands (id, whoami, curl, /dev/tcp, base64) confirm RCE; a routine deploy/healthcheck string does not. Confirm the host runs Flowise <3.1.3. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the node process tree, and rotate any credentials/API keys the service account could read (Flowise DB, LLM provider keys). 3) Hunt: review preceding /api/v1/prediction POSTs (UC1) for the injection payload and outbound connections from node-descended interpreters (UC3); check for new cron/systemd persistence written by the shell.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "flowise"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, ProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "flowise"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh") or ActingProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reverse shell / egress from Flowise node-spawned interpreter (CVE-2026-70477 post-exploit) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects an interpreter or transfer tool (bash/python/nc/socat/curl/wget) spawned under the Flowise Node.js process making an outbound connection to a public IP — the reverse-shell and exfil stage the PoC exposes via its --r_host/--r_port/--cmd options after CSV Agent RCE. Rationale: Targets the PoC's reverse-shell/exec surface (--r_host/--r_port/--l_port/--cmd) by keying on interpreters spawned by the Flowise `node` parent that either connect to a public IP (Defender network telemetry) or carry classic reverse-shell command lines (/dev/tcp, pty.spawn, -e /bin/sh). Distinct network pivot from UC2's process-spawn logic. Datadog/Sigma omitted: the required parent-process ancestry plus network correlation isn't expressible on the available Datadog auditd schema or a single-event Sigma shape. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elttam.com/blog/cruising-for-shells-in-flowise • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/flowise-components/CVE-2026-70477/

1) Triage: inspect the interpreter's command line and RemoteIP/RemotePort — a listener callback (matching a recently-seen external IP) or /dev/tcp redirection confirms a reverse shell; a known package mirror is benign. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the node process tree, and firewall the destination IP; rotate the service account and any secrets reachable from it. 3) Hunt: correlate with the originating /api/v1/prediction POST (UC1) and node→shell spawn (UC2) on the same host in the surrounding minutes, and sweep other Flowise instances for the same RemoteIP.

Chrome launched with DevTools/remote-debugging port by shell launcher (XCSSET v40 browser hijack) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the XCSSET v40 Chrome hijacker, which wraps the legitimate Google Chrome binary in a malicious launcher script and starts it with Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) enabled on a local port to fetch attacker JavaScript, intercept cookies/credentials, and manipulate MetaMask transactions. Detection keys on Chrome being started with --remote-debugging-port/--remote-debugging-pipe by a shell/osascript parent rather than the user's Finder/launchd session. Rationale: Uses the article's specific Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) hijack behaviour plus Unit 42's detail that the module wraps the Chrome binary in a malicious launcher; the shell/osascript-or-/tmp parent + non-headless remote-debugging flag is the fidelity anchor that separates it from developer automation. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/xcsset-v40-malware-analysis/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/xcsset-v40-abuses-chrome-devtools/ • https://gbhackers.com/xcsset-v40-infects-xcode-projects/
ATT&CKT1185 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running Puppeteer/Playwright/Selenium end-to-end tests that spawn Chrome with a debugging port (usually --headless, filtered)
  • QA/automation harness launched from a shell script for UI testing
  • Browser extension developer manually starting Chrome with --remote-debugging-port for local debugging
  • Electron/CEF app tooling invoking Chromium with a debugging port from a wrapper shell
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("puppeteer","playwright","selenium","chromedriver") and ProcessCommandLine !has "--headless"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and the launcher script path (/tmp or /var/folders) — a legit debug session comes from a known dev tool, XCSSET's launcher is an ad hoc-signed script in a temp path. Check the same host's DeviceNetworkEvents for the XCSSET C2 domains/IPs. 2) Contain: kill the Chrome + launcher process, isolate the host, and force a Chrome profile/cookie + password reset (session cookies and MetaMask data are assumed stolen). 3) Hunt: search for /tmp/r, /tmp/p.app, ~/.tr and tccutil reset / CloudTelemetryService activity on the host and across other developer endpoints that pulled the same Xcode project/repo.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "Google Chrome" or FolderPath has "Google Chrome.app"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "--headless"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","osascript") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/tmp/" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/var/folders/"
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("puppeteer","playwright","selenium","chromedriver"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has "Google Chrome"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine !has "--headless"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("bash","zsh","sh","osascript") or ParentProcessName has_any ("/tmp/","/var/folders/")
| where not(ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("puppeteer","playwright","selenium","chromedriver"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

macOS security tooling sabotage: tccutil reset + CloudTelemetryService kill + XProtect/softwareupdate tamper (XCSSET v40) AIInstallation High
Hunts XCSSET v40's aggressive defense-evasion stage that resets the TCC database (tccutil reset AppleEvents), terminates Apple's CloudTelemetryService, disables Gatekeeper (spctl), and blocks XProtect/MRT updates via the SoftwareUpdate channel. These commands rarely co-occur in normal user activity and are a strong, article-specific signal. Rationale: Anchors on Unit 42's verbatim evasion actions — tccutil reset AppleEvents, killing CloudTelemetryService, and blocking XProtect/MRT via the SoftwareUpdate channel — which are individually rare and collectively near-unique to this malware's teardown of macOS defenses. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/xcsset-v40-malware-analysis/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/xcsset-v40-abuses-chrome-devtools/ • https://gbhackers.com/xcsset-v40-infects-xcode-projects/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1553.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin/support running 'tccutil reset' to fix a stuck privacy prompt
  • Developer disabling Gatekeeper with spctl --master-disable to test an unsigned build
  • MDM/management tooling adjusting SoftwareUpdate/XProtect settings during patch policy changes
  • Troubleshooting scripts killing Apple daemons to clear a hung telemetry/update state
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/folders/") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("osascript","bash","sh","zsh")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent process — legit admin actions come from Terminal/osascript run by a known admin, XCSSET's come from /tmp or /var/folders loaders; check whether tccutil reset, CloudTelemetryService kill, and XProtect tamper cluster within minutes on one host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, re-enable Gatekeeper (spctl --master-enable), and treat the endpoint as fully compromised (defenses were deliberately blinded). 3) Hunt: pivot on /tmp/r, /tmp/p.app, Chrome remote-debugging launches, and the C2 IOCs; check other developers who cloned the same Xcode project/GitHub repo.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (FileName =~ "tccutil" and ProcessCommandLine has "reset")
    or (FileName in~ ("killall","pkill","kill") and ProcessCommandLine has "CloudTelemetryService")
    or (FileName =~ "spctl" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--master-disable","--global-disable"))
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "softwareupdate" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("XProtect","XProtectFramework","MRTConfigData"))
    or ProcessCommandLine has "CloudTelemetryService"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (TargetProcessName has "tccutil" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "reset")
    or (TargetProcessName has_any ("killall","pkill") and TargetProcessCommandLine has "CloudTelemetryService")
    or (TargetProcessName has "spctl" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--master-disable","--global-disable"))
    or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "softwareupdate" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("XProtect","MRTConfigData"))
    or TargetProcessCommandLine has "CloudTelemetryService"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

XCSSET v40 C2 beacon to Unit 42 IOC domains / IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections and DNS lookups from macOS hosts to the XCSSET v40 command-and-control domains and IPs published by Unit 42. High-confidence IOC match confirmed by multiple second sources reporting the same campaign infrastructure. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the article's pre-extracted C2 domains and IPs, cross-confirmed against the Unit 42 report and secondary write-ups; the impersonation theme (apple*/amzn*/cdn* on .ru/.in TLDs) matches the campaign's fake-CDN infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/xcsset-v40-malware-analysis/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/xcsset-v40-abuses-chrome-devtools/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or sandbox detonating an XCSSET sample from a corporate network
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively resolving IOC domains for validation
  • A sinkholed domain now resolving to a benign parking IP (validate the resolved IP)
  • Typosquat collision where a benign internal tool happens to query a lookalike CDN domain (rare)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the endpoint (DeviceNetworkEvents InitiatingProcessFileName) — expect osascript, a /tmp loader, or the wrapped Chrome; confirm the host isn't a sandbox/research box. 2) Contain: block the domains/IPs at proxy+firewall, isolate the host, and revoke any credentials/session cookies used from it. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for the full IOC set, and pull the XCSSET on-host artifacts (/tmp/r, /tmp/p.app, ~/.tr, tccutil/CloudTelemetryService tamper) to scope the intrusion and find the source Xcode project.
let c2domains = dynamic(["amzndev.in","amzndev.ru","googlenets.ru","netcdndev.in","whitead.in","whiteads.ru","accapple.ru","adschecks.ru","adsmobi.ru","adsmorein.in","adsmoreme.in","amdcdn.ru","amznprod.in","applecdn.ru","appledisk.ru","appledns.ru","applehosts.ru","appletime.in","bulksec.ru","cdnamz.in"]);
let c2ips = dynamic(["91.108.106.229","95.142.35.34","95.142.35.206","95.142.37.159","151.243.109.188","178.208.92.129","178.208.92.168"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (c2ips) or RemoteUrl has_any (c2domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2domains = dynamic(["amzndev.in","amzndev.ru","googlenets.ru","netcdndev.in","whitead.in","whiteads.ru","accapple.ru","adschecks.ru","adsmobi.ru","adsmorein.in","adsmoreme.in","amdcdn.ru","amznprod.in","applecdn.ru","appledisk.ru","appledns.ru","applehosts.ru","appletime.in","bulksec.ru","cdnamz.in"]);
let c2ips = dynamic(["91.108.106.229","95.142.35.34","95.142.35.206","95.142.37.159","151.243.109.188","178.208.92.129","178.208.92.168"]);
union
 (ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has_any (c2domains) | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Indicator = DnsQuery, Kind = "dns"),
 (ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr in (c2ips) | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Indicator = DstIpAddr, Kind = "network")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

XCSSET v40 Telegram trojanizer: /Applications/Telegram.app replacement + ~/.tr config drop AIInstallation High
Hunts the XCSSET v40 Telegram trojanizer, which deletes the legitimate Telegram Desktop app, drops a C2-controlled ad hoc-signed replacement into /Applications/Telegram.app, and writes its state to ~/.tr and ~/.tr_map. Detection keys on non-Telegram, shell/downloader processes modifying the Telegram bundle plus the malware's hidden config files. Rationale: Uses Unit 42's exact artifacts — the /Applications/Telegram.app replacement plus the ~/.tr and ~/.tr_map config files — and requires a shell/downloader (not Telegram's own updater) as the acting process, which is what distinguishes the trojanization from a legitimate Telegram update. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/xcsset-v40-malware-analysis/ • https://gbhackers.com/xcsset-v40-infects-xcode-projects/
ATT&CKT1554 T1553.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Telegram Desktop self-update (filtered — acting process is Telegram/softwareupdated, not a shell)
  • User reinstalling Telegram by unzipping a downloaded DMG/zip via Finder/ditto
  • Homebrew cask upgrade of telegram writing to /Applications/Telegram.app
  • Backup/sync tool touching the Telegram bundle path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Telegram","softwareupdated","installd") and (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/tmp/" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/var/folders/" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("osascript","curl","ditto"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the acting process and command line — a shell/curl/osascript from /tmp writing the Telegram bundle is malicious; verify code signature of the resulting /Applications/Telegram.app (XCSSET's is ad hoc-signed, not Apple/Telegram Developer ID). 2) Contain: kill the process, quarantine the trojanized Telegram.app and ~/.tr*, isolate the host, and warn the user their Telegram session may be intercepted. 3) Hunt: correlate with the Chrome remote-debugging hijack, tccutil/CloudTelemetryService tamper, and C2 IOCs on the same host; check other developer machines for the same Telegram.app replacement pattern.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (FolderPath has "/Applications/Telegram.app" and ActionType in ("FileDeleted","FileRenamed","FileCreated","FileModified"))
    or FileName in~ (".tr",".tr_map")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","osascript","curl","ditto","unzip","tar") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/tmp/" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/var/folders/"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Telegram","softwareupdated","installd","Install Telegram")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (TargetFilePath has "/Applications/Telegram.app") or TargetFileName in~ (".tr",".tr_map")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","zsh","osascript","curl","ditto","unzip","tar") or ActingProcessName has_any ("/tmp/","/var/folders/")
| where ActingProcessName !has "Telegram"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

XCSSET v40 build-time execution: Xcode-spawned osascript loader / /tmp/r payload AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the XCSSET v40 initial execution that triggers when a developer builds a compromised Xcode project: an injected script launches an in-memory osascript loader that pulls the orchestrator, and the malware stages a loader at /tmp/r and an AppleScript wrapper at /tmp/p.app. Detection keys on Xcode/xcodebuild spawning osascript, or any process referencing the /tmp/r and /tmp/p.app loader paths. Rationale: Uses Unit 42's verbatim loader paths (/tmp/r primary loader, /tmp/p.app AppleScript wrapper) and the article's core mechanic that an in-memory osascript loader runs when a poisoned Xcode project is built; osascript spawned by Xcode/xcodebuild is abnormal for normal build phases (which use /bin/sh). Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/xcsset-v40-malware-analysis/ • https://gbhackers.com/xcsset-v40-infects-xcode-projects/
ATT&CKT1059.002 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Xcode build 'Run Script' phase that intentionally calls osascript (e.g. to display a notification)
  • Developer tooling or Fastlane lanes invoking osascript during a build
  • A benign local script that happens to use a /tmp/r or /tmp/p.app path name (rare)
  • CI runner on macOS executing AppleScript automation as part of packaging
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "osascript" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("fastlane","display notification","display dialog"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the osascript command line and parent Xcode project path; dump /tmp/r and /tmp/p.app for analysis and check the project's benign files/Git hooks for the injected downloader script. 2) Contain: isolate the developer host, kill the loader chain, and freeze the source repository/branch to stop propagation to other developers. 3) Hunt: identify every developer who cloned or built the same project/repo, and sweep those hosts for the Chrome hijack, Telegram replacement, security-tamper commands, and C2 IOCs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/r","/tmp/p.app")
    or FolderPath in~ ("/tmp/r")
    or (FileName =~ "osascript" and (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("xcodebuild","Xcode") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "Xcode.app"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/r","/tmp/p.app")
    or (TargetProcessName has "osascript" and (ParentProcessName has_any ("xcodebuild","Xcode") or ParentProcessName has "Xcode.app"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
